messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thanh is a 44-year-old Vietnamese American man who has been married for sixteen years and works as a registered nurse at a busy urban hospital. He presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after being mugged at knifepoint in a parking garage near his workplace. It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn, and Thanh had just finished a twelve-hour shift. He was walking to his car when a man stepped out from behind a concrete pillar, pressed a blade against his ribs, and demanded his wallet and phone. The attacker shoved him hard against a parked car before running off, and Thanh stood alone in the dim fluorescent light for several minutes, unable to move, his side aching where the knife had pressed into him. He had not been cut, but the pressure of the blade had left a bruise that lasted two weeks — and a physical imprint that, he would later discover, had not faded at all.

In the weeks that followed, Thanh found that the memory did not behave like ordinary recollection. It returned not as a narrative but as a sequence of still images: the attacker's face illuminated from below by a phone screen, the silver glint of the blade, the yellow-grey concrete of the pillar. These images arrived without warning and with a quality he described as photographic — precise, flat, and inescapable. More distressing still, each time the memory surfaced he felt a sharp ache in his left side, exactly where the knife had pressed, as though the bruise had never healed. These intrusive, embodied memories began to reinforce something darker in how Thanh understood what had happened to him. He had come to believe, with a quiet but unshakeable conviction, that something about him had invited the attack — that he had been too slow, too visible, too trusting — and that this quality, whatever it was, had not gone away. He was certain that nothing good lay ahead of him now, and that the future he had imagined for himself and his wife had been foreclosed. These appraisals were not fleeting; they had settled into him like a diagnosis.

It was this belief in his own fundamental vulnerability that drove the behaviours that now structured his days. Convinced that the world remained actively dangerous and that he was specifically susceptible to harm, Thanh began scanning every environment he entered with methodical intensity. At the hospital, where he spent most of his waking hours, he chose seats in the break room that placed his back against a wall and offered a clear view of both doors. He checked behind himself repeatedly when walking the corridors between wards, and when he used the staff bathroom he checked the mirror before leaving, then checked it again. He kept his mind occupied with mental tasks — reciting medication dosages, rehearsing patient schedules — anything to prevent the stillness in which the images returned. But this relentless vigilance, rather than providing relief, kept the threat feeling immediate and unresolved. The heightened alertness meant that ordinary sounds — a door slamming, a trolley wheeled quickly down a corridor — registered as potential danger, and each such moment pulled the photographic memories back to the surface with fresh urgency. His sleep had deteriorated badly; he lay awake most nights rehearsing exits and scanning the sounds of the apartment building, and arrived at his shifts already exhausted.

The strategies that were meant to protect him were, in their own way, sustaining the very appraisals they were designed to manage. Because he never allowed himself to be still, he never discovered that the threat was not constant — and the belief that something intrinsic to him made him a target remained untested and intact. His wife had noticed the changes and had begun to gently withdraw from conversations about his work, uncertain how to reach him. Colleagues had remarked that he seemed distracted, and he had been passed over for a charge nurse opportunity he had worked toward for years, a loss he absorbed as confirmation that his future had indeed closed.

What finally brought Thanh to seek help was a morning when he could not enter the hospital parking garage. He stood at its entrance for eleven minutes before turning around. He was most afraid, he said quietly in the intake session, that this was simply who he was now — and most hoping, in a voice that carried considerable doubt, that it was not.
